analysis.one_liner: Cuts the estate tax rate to 30% and exempts the first $10 million of an estate from tax.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2005 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2007 without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would permanently cut the federal estate and gift tax rate to 30% and shield the first $10 million of every estate from tax, with that amount rising with inflation. It would also raise the annual tax-free gift limit from $10,000 to $50,000 per recipient. The change would apply only to very large estates, since almost no estates are worth more than $10 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth more than $10 million, who would pay a lower rate on whatever is left above that threshold and would owe nothing at all on estates under $10 million. Wealthy families that plan large lifetime gifts would also benefit from the higher $50,000 annual gift allowance.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a flat 30% rate on the taxable estate, replacing the higher graduated rates then scheduled to return after the 2001 tax law's temporary repeal expired.
It raises the unified credit so the first $10 million of an estate is tax-free, adjusted for inflation after 2005.
It raises the annual gift tax exclusion from $10,000 to $50,000 per recipient, letting wealthy families transfer far more money during life without tax.
It makes these changes permanent by repealing the provisions of the 2001 tax law that would have brought back the old estate tax rules after 2010.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax raises billions of dollars a year from the largest estates; cutting its rate and exempting the first $10 million reduces that revenue, which means either less money for government services or more borrowing.

drawbacks.text: The benefits flow almost entirely to the largest estates. Estates under $10 million — the overwhelming majority — would already owe no estate tax, so the exclusion increase gives them nothing new while giving multimillion-dollar estates a large tax cut.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the revenue cost: reducing the rate to 30% and exempting the first $10 million shrinks a tax paid only by a small share of the very largest estates, reducing federal revenue that otherwise funds programs serving everyone.
Defenders of the estate tax argue it falls on inherited wealth that has never been taxed to the recipient; cutting it shifts the tax burden toward wages and work income.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: a handful of the largest family fortunes would save millions of dollars each. The cost is diffuse: less federal revenue from the estates best able to pay, borne by everyone else through services or debt. Even supporters of estate tax relief generally focused on protecting family farms and small businesses, and a $10 million exemption already shields nearly all of those — making the additional rate cut and gift-tax expansion hard to justify on revenue terms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Representative Jim Leach introduced the bill on April 12, 2005, joined by Representatives John Tanner and Neil Abercrombie.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles all tax legislation.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, no estate tax cut took effect; large estates and their heirs remained subject to the tax as it stood, and the federal treasury kept the revenue the bill would have forgone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue; no tax cut took effect

for.name: Rep. Jim Leach
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the estate tax rate to 30% and raise the exclusion to $10 million.

for.name: Rep. John Tanner and Rep. Neil Abercrombie
for.what_they_did: Joined the Republican sponsor in introducing the bill; the bill finished with three cosponsors (two Democrats, one Republican).

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearings, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Estate tax cuts were a Republican priority in this era; the bill's only cosponsorship support beyond the sponsor came from two Democrats, but no committee or floor action followed.

industries.note: Heirs to estates over $10 million would pay sharply less tax, and the higher gift exclusion would let the wealthy pass on money tax-free during life. The cost is federal revenue borne by everyone else.

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers and wealth advisers
industries.note: A higher gift exclusion and new exemption thresholds would create planning work around large tax-free transfers, though a permanent, simpler 30% rate reduces some complexity-driven business.
